title: The Moonbeam Rescue
markdown:
As the sun slipped below the hills and left the sky lavender and rose, Dara the pond skater swirled on water as still as held breath. His legs were long and light, made for that quiet dance. He loved this hush, just before the stars began their silent games. Beside the mossy bank sat Nib the moon rabbit, fur the colour of a misty morning, ears listening for the whisper-sounds of night.

It was the eve of the Festival of Whispering Lights. The moon, a silvery disc, peeked over the tallest pine. Its glow spilled down — and with a soft shimmering plop a piece of that reflection tumbled into the pond. The fallen moonbeam pulsed, cool as river silk, bright as swallowed starlight, and smelling faintly of frost and wet reed. Ice began to form a thin fragile shell around it.

“The moon-glow has fallen,” Dara murmured. “And look. Ice.”

Nib’s nose twitched. “The glow-worms and fireflies use the moon’s reflection to find their way. If it stays under ice, they will wander.”

They made a pact, small and serious as a held-out paw: they would return the light before the festival lamps were lit. The condition was simple. Do not smash the ice. Shatter it, and the glow would scatter into crumbs no one could gather.

For a little while they lived with the companion in secrecy, skating and sitting near the pulse, telling no one on the far bank. The moonbeam seemed almost a creature, lonely and bright.

Then Dara, eager, asked the ice a question it could not answer — he pressed too hard with a skate, testing, hurrying. A crack ran. The taboo broke. The moonbeam sank a finger deeper. The ice thickened with a quiet that felt like lament.

“We promised,” Nib whispered.

The quest began.

First impossible task: still the ripples without force. Dara glided in slower and slower circles until the water forgot to shiver. Kindness, not speed.

Second: warm the edge without breaking it. Nib breathed, soft as falling petals, until a narrow seam loosened like a smile.

Third: invite, do not grab. The glow-worms came then, secret helpers, tiny lamps along the reeds. Fireflies blinked a path. Dara whispered, “Just a little further. It looks so lonely.” Nib hopped as if the ice were a sleeping friend.

At the brightest centre Dara set himself just so. “Now.”

Nib’s pale paw brushed the luminous light. They did not seize. They encouraged. Slowly the shimmering pearl lifted, pulled free, and rose to rejoin its mother in the sky with a silent silvery sigh. In that one colourful moment the trapped glow became the moon again, whole and high, and the ice melted to smooth clear water.

Glow-worms twinkled. Fireflies blinked home. Dara, who had hurried, felt properly small and glad. Nib’s ears eased.

The festival air shimmered. They nestled at the pond’s edge, watching moonbeams dance, listening to the night’s hum. Soon the little creatures were tucked in, and Dara and Nib drifted toward sleep under the moon’s steady shine.

Thus a promise kept, even after a crack, can carry a friend home to their true light.
characters: Dara (a pond skater), Nib (a moon rabbit)
author: StoryGen Community
